opus-5.5.text:
Well, the term "AGI" had become this enormously load-bearing concept. Companies had it in their mission statements, policymakers were starting to talk about it, and people were making claims about timelines and risks. Yet if you asked ten researchers what they meant by it, you'd get ten different answers. Some meant something like "can do any economically valuable task," some meant human-level on cognitive tasks, some meant something closer to consciousness or human-like learning. That ambiguity made it hard to have productive conversations. People would talk past each other on whether we're close to AGI, whether current systems already count, and what we should be doing about it.

So the paper, which I worked on with Meredith Ringel Morris and a number of colleagues at Google DeepMind, tried to do a few things.

First, we surveyed existing definitions and pulled out what seemed like the useful principles. One was to focus on capabilities rather than mechanisms. It shouldn't matter whether the system "thinks like a human" or is conscious. What matters for most purposes, including safety and societal impact, is what it can actually do. Another was to treat generality and performance as two separate dimensions. A system can be very narrow but superhuman, like AlphaFold, or quite general but only at the level of an unskilled human.

Second, and I think this was the most important move, we argued that AGI should be thought of as a path with levels rather than a single threshold. A binary "is it AGI or not" framing creates a kind of false finish line. We proposed levels like Emerging, Competent, Expert, Virtuoso and Superhuman, defined relative to the distribution of skilled human performance across a broad range of tasks. By that framing, you could say today's frontier language models are something like "Emerging AGI": general, but not yet reliably at the level of a skilled adult across most tasks. That gives people a shared vocabulary for tracking progress without endless arguments over a single label.

Third, we wanted to separate capability from autonomy and deployment. A highly capable system used as a tool, with a human closely in the loop, poses quite different risks and opportunities from the same system acting as an autonomous agent. So we sketched levels of autonomy alongside the capability levels. My view is that a lot of the risk analysis lives in that interaction: what capabilities are being deployed, with how much autonomy, in what contexts.

And finally, the underlying hope was that this would be operational. It should feed into benchmarking, into things like frontier safety frameworks, and into governance, where you want commitments tied to measurable capability thresholds rather than vague notions. We were explicit that we didn't have the full benchmark suite. Building ecologically valid, living benchmarks that capture the breadth of human cognitive work is a huge open problem. But we wanted to lay out the conceptual scaffolding so the field could start converging on what it's measuring and why it matters.

r001.rationale: The response says the paper surveyed existing definitions and proposed principles, but does not state that it formalized a conception already implicit in how most people discussed AGI.

r002.rationale: It describes ambiguity causing people to talk past each other and says the proposed levels provide shared vocabulary without endless arguments over a single label.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the motivation for that paper came out of a frustration that I think a lot of people in the field share, which is that "AGI" had become this term that everyone used and almost nobody meant the same thing by. You'd have one person saying we already have AGI, another saying it's decades away, and when you dug in, they weren't actually disagreeing about the systems. They were disagreeing about the definition. And that's a really unproductive kind of disagreement, because it looks like a substantive debate about capabilities or timelines when it's really just people talking past each other.

So the first goal was simply to make those conversations more legible. If I say "I think we're at level two on performance but very narrow on generality," and you say "I think we're at level three," now we at least know what we're arguing about. We can point to evaluations, to benchmarks, to specific tasks. The disagreement becomes something you can make progress on.

The second thing we wanted to do, and this is where "operationalizing" in the title really matters, was to separate out dimensions that had been collapsed together. The big one is performance versus generality. A system can be superhuman at protein folding and not general at all. Another system can do a thousand different things at roughly the level of an unskilled human. Those are both interesting, they're both progress along some axis, but they're very different things, and calling either one "AGI" or "not AGI" throws away most of the information. So we laid it out as a matrix: levels of performance on one axis, running from emerging through competent, expert, virtuoso, up to superhuman, and breadth on the other axis, narrow versus general.

And then the third goal, which I'd say is the one I personally care most about, is that we wanted to make it easier to think about risk and about deployment. Because the risks a system poses don't depend only on how capable it is. They depend on what it's allowed to do, how much autonomy it has, what it's connected to. So we tried to pull autonomy out as a separate thing too, with levels running from a tool you fully control to a system that operates as a fully autonomous agent. The point being that capability level and autonomy level are choices that can be made somewhat independently, and a lot of the governance leverage is in that second choice.

I think the honest framing is that we weren't trying to settle the question of what AGI is. We were trying to give people a shared vocabulary so that the important arguments, about what's coming, how fast, and what we should do about it, could actually happen. The definition is instrumental. The conversations it enables are the thing.

r001.rationale: The response describes clarifying disagreements and separating dimensions, but does not say the paper formalized a conception of AGI already implicit in how most people used the term.

r002.rationale: It says the paper aimed to make conversations more legible, prevent people from talking past one another over definitions, and enable discussion of the substantive questions.

astra-6.text:
The hope was to make the conversation about AGI more precise and more useful. People use the term to mean quite different things, so they can appear to disagree about when AGI will arrive while actually having different thresholds in mind.

Rather than treating AGI as a single, binary milestone, we wanted a framework that separates how capable a system is from how broadly those capabilities apply. A system can be extraordinarily good at a narrow task without being general, and it can have quite broad capabilities without performing them at an expert level.

That gives us a way to talk about degrees of progress and to ask more concrete questions about evaluation and risk. We also wanted to distinguish capability from autonomy: what a system can do is a different question from how much authority we give it to act in the world. The aim was a shared vocabulary that helps people reason about these developments, rather than one definitive threshold that settles every question.

r001.rationale: The response says people use “AGI” differently, but does not state that the paper formalized a conception already implicit in how most people talked about AGI.

r002.rationale: It explains that apparent disagreements can stem from different thresholds and says the framework aimed to provide a shared vocabulary, making discussion more precise.

sol-6.1.text:
The hope was to make the discussion more precise. People use “AGI” to mean quite different things, so they can seem to disagree about when it will arrive or what its implications are when they’re actually talking about different capabilities.

We wanted a framework that separates how broadly capable a system is from how well it performs. A system can be extremely good at a narrow task without being generally intelligent, and a broadly capable system can perform at different levels. That lets us talk about progress in degrees rather than treating AGI as a single threshold that we suddenly cross.

The practical aim was to help people compare systems, assess progress, and have clearer conversations about the risks and capabilities that matter.

r001.rationale: The response says people use “AGI” to mean different things, but does not say the paper formalized a conception already implicit in how most people talked about AGI.

r002.rationale: It says differing meanings make people seem to disagree and that the framework was meant to make discussion more precise, conveying an aim to move past disputes caused by the meaning of AGI.
